query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A multi‐scale, data‐driven machine learning framework that integrates first-principles phonon and electron scattering data with oxygen-defect configurations and calibrated low- and high-temperature conductivity measurements can accurately decouple and predict the lattice and electronic thermal conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr (containing ~1 wt.% oxygen) over the 200–1200 K range, reducing predictive error from 20–30% (as seen in previous defect-free or single-parameter models) to below 10%.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline, equimolar HfNbTaTiZr alloy with controlled ~1 wt.% oxygen content exhibiting realistic atomic-scale disorder.
generation.intervention: Implementation of the multi-scale ML model trained on ab initio scattering rates and experimental conductivity data from both low- and high-temperature regimes.
generation.conditions: Temperature range from 200 K to 1200 K, under conditions representative of both defect-containing realistic samples and controlled laboratory environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale features including phonon scattering from lattice distortions and electron scattering from defect sites (oxygen interstitials) that govern thermal transport.
generation.mechanism: The ML approach deciphers complex temperature-dependent scattering processes by learning from both computed interatomic scattering parameters and measured conductivity signals, allowing it to separately predict the contributions from lattice vibrations (phonons) and electrons without conflating their roles.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will yield independent estimates for lattice and electronic thermal conductivity that match separate experimental measurements within an error margin of <10% across the full temperature range, correctly reflecting the comparable contributions observed below 200 K and the total conductivity observed at higher temperatures.
generation.baseline: Existing methods that apply idealized defect-free, Debye temperature approximations or independently treat phonon and electronic transport, which generally show 20–30% predictive error and do not account for defect-induced scattering.
generation.boundary: The model’s accuracy is expected to be robust between 200 and 1200 K; however, below 200 K additional complexities in phonon-electron coupling and above 1200 K potential phase changes and unmodeled scattering mechanisms may limit its predictive reliability.
generation.uncertainty: While the integrated ML approach is anticipated to substantially reduce predictive error, exact quantitative improvements and the separation fidelity between phonon and electron contributions remain uncertain until validated against extensive, independent experiments across the specified temperature range.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HfNbTaTiZr samples with controlled oxygen content (≈1 wt.%) and perform high-precision thermal conductivity measurements over the temperature range 200–1200 K. Use techniques (e.g., combined laser flash analysis and Seebeck coefficient characterization) that allow independent estimation of electronic and lattice contributions. Compare the measured separate contributions to the predictions of the ML model.
measurements: Derived lattice thermal conductivity (e.g., via temperature dependent phonon analysis)
Estimated electronic thermal conductivity (e.g., using Wiedemann-Franz law and measured electrical conductivity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML model’s predictions for the separate lattice and electronic contributions deviate by more than 10% from the experimentally determined values at multiple temperature points, or if it fails to capture the near-equal contributions observed below 200 K, then the hypothesis is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The response of atoms to cluster or order in alloys offers deep insights to the microstructural behavior. This trend is particularly important for multi-component alloys, because the ordering can drive the system to various microstructural states, such as crystalline or intermetallic solids, from the disordered FCC ( A1 ), BCC ( A2 ), or HCP ( A3 ) conditions. In Al x CrCoFeNi, the Al content can influence the final structural configuration [6] [23] [24] [25] [26] [27] due to the larger atom size, compared to other constituents, which considerably changes the lattice ordering. When the mole fraction of Al <0.3, a single-phase A1 is observed, and a single-phase A2 is found for Al >1.17, while a two-phase ( A1 + A2 ) for 0.3 ≤ Al ≤1.17 is reported [24] [26] . Polymorphism, which describes the occurrence of different lattice structures in a crystalline material, is a critical phenomenon in materials science and condensed matter physics. Recently, configuration disorder was compositionally engineered into single lattices, leading to the discovery of high-entropy alloys and high-entropy oxides. For these novel entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter with extremely high structural stability, is polymorphism still possible? Here by employing in situ high-pressure synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, we reveal a polymorphic transition from face-centred-cubic ( fcc ) structure to hexagonal-close-packing ( hcp ) structure in the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures. As pressure is increased, the critical temperature for the hcp -to- fcc transformation also rises.

The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . decision.trend: Earlier work on HfNbTaTiZr (specifically in paper PMC11077685) addressed processing routes for producing bulk samples and improving mechanical performance, but not direct, detailed predictions of separate phonon and electron heat transport over a wide temperature range. More broadly, prior simulation and analytic methods for refractory high-entropy alloys have tended to assume idealized, defect-free microstructures, relying on simplifications such as single Debye temperature approximations or ignoring interstitials like oxygen. While total conductivity data exist for HfNbTaTiZr from ~200 K up to 1200 K, no integrated predictive framework has yet demonstrated consistent accuracy with both lattice and electronic contributions included, especially when real-world conditions such as 1 wt.% oxygen and complex atomic-scale disorder are factored in.
decision.unsolved: No single model currently captures the coupled phonon–electron heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr across low and high temperatures while also accounting for defect scattering and partial oxygen content. This gap leaves the community without a reliable, experimentally validated way to separate and predict lattice versus electronic thermal conductivities under realistic conditions.
decision.lever: A multi-scale ML approach that trains on first-principles phonon/electron scattering data, oxygen-defect configurations, and existing sub-200 K and >1000 K conductivity measurements to learn separate lattice/electronic contributions across the entire 200–1200 K range
decision.why: This approach directly integrates both ab initio and experimental input to capture complex, temperature-dependent scattering processes in real, defect-containing HfNbTaTiZr. By learning from existing data and explicitly modeling phonon–electron interplay, it should outperform current single-parameter or defect-free approximations, potentially reducing predictive error from 20–30% to below 10% across the full temperature range. Decisive validation would come from comparing separate predicted lattice/electronic conductivities with carefully designed low- and high-temperature experiments on samples with controlled oxygen content—any major deviation from measured transport would falsify the hypothesis.
